rationale: The plasma samples come from two acquisition batches, and Orbitrap batches usually shift each protein's intensity in a systematic way. Those shifts can hide the disease signal or be mistaken for it. I now subtract each protein's median within its batch before imputing, using only training-fold rows of that batch. This is ComBat-style location correction, so the regularized logistic regression sees within-batch biology.

In DIA plasma data, whether a protein gets quantified depends on its abundance, so a protein that drops out of detection can itself carry disease signal. The current 70% filter and half-minimum fill throw most of that away. I'm adding binary "detected" flags for proteins quantified in 30–95% of training samples. Each flag is centred within its batch using training rows only, so batch differences in detection rates are removed, and the flags are down-weighted to 0.5 so they don't swamp the intensity features in the same L2 logistic regression.

Plasma proteomes vary a lot with how each sample was handled. Red-cell lysis, platelet carry-over and partial clotting each shift hundreds of proteins together (the Geyer et al. contamination panels), and that noise can hide the AD signal. Using only the training fold, this version builds three label-free contamination scores from marker proteins (erythrocyte, platelet and coagulation panels). It then regresses those scores out of each protein's observed log intensities after batch correction and before imputation, so the L2 logistic regression only sees variation that is unrelated to sample quality. I haven't run it yet; the 0.900 baseline is the previous round's score.

Plasma DIA intensities have heavy tails: one sample with an acute-phase response, a haemolysis spike or a half-minimum fill can sit 5–10 SD out on a protein. With n≈89 and about 1,000 features, a few such points can pull the L2 logistic weights a long way. This change clips each standardized feature to ±3 SD, using bounds from the training fold, so the model learns from shifts shared by many samples rather than from single-sample extremes.

Right now a protein passes the filter if it is quantified in at least 70% of all training samples. That lets in proteins seen in nearly every sample of one batch but only rarely in the other. For those proteins, the half-minimum fill puts a batch-specific block of imputed values into the data, and the per-batch median correction, which uses only observed values, doesn't remove it. The model can then learn batch artifacts instead of biology. This change requires a protein to be quantified in at least 70% of training samples within every batch that has 5 or more training rows, so only proteins measured consistently across acquisitions are kept.

Right now each sample is median-centred over whatever proteins it happened to quantify, so a sample measured more deeply (more low-abundance proteins detected) gets a lower median, and all of its proteins shift up. That is a run-depth/batch artefact, not biology. This change centres each sample on the median of a fixed reference set instead: proteins quantified in at least 95% of all samples. The reference set is chosen without labels, so the normalisation no longer depends on how many proteins each sample happened to quantify.

With n≈71 per training fold and about 1,000 correlated proteins, the best single L2 strength is poorly identified, and tuning C with inner CV at this sample size would itself be noisy. Instead I average the predicted probabilities of L2 logistic regressions over a fixed C grid (0.01–0.3). The ensemble then mixes models that sit close to the class-mean difference with models that use more of the covariance, which should make the ranking less sensitive to where any one fold lands. I'm averaging probabilities rather than ranks so the out-of-fold scores stay comparable when they're pooled across folds. I haven't run this yet, so I don't have a Dev score for it.

Of the ~1,000 proteins that pass the filter in each fold, most probably carry no AD signal, yet each one still adds noise to the L2 logistic regression when only ~71 training samples are available. This version ranks proteins by Welch t-statistic on the training fold only (after batch correction, scaling and clipping) and keeps the top 300 before fitting. I chose 300 in advance as a moderate cut: it keeps the model looking at a broad multi-protein signature without relying on a noisy small panel, and I did not tune it against the Dev score. I haven't run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Instead of the half-minimum fill, I impute missing values with kNN (k=5) in train-standardised space. Neighbours come from training samples only. Proteins that pass the ≥70% per-batch detection filter are abundant enough that their DIA-NN dropouts are mostly identification/FDR misses rather than values below the detection limit. Filling them at min−1 creates fake extreme points that sit at the −3 SD clip and pull the L2 weights. kNN uses co-varying proteins to fill in plausible values instead.

Round 1 corrected batch location only, but separate Orbitrap Astral acquisitions also often differ in dynamic range and noise for each protein. That puts one batch's samples further out once features are standardised globally. Using training-fold rows only, I'll rescale each protein within each batch by its robust (MAD) SD relative to the pooled within-batch SD. The scale ratio is shrunk toward 1 in log space, ComBat-style, so the logistic regression sees within-batch biological variation on one common scale. I haven't run this yet, so there is no Dev score for it.

Lower the L2 penalty on a fixed list of known AD and neurodegeneration plasma proteins by multiplying their standardised, clipped features by 2. This is the same as a 4× weaker penalty on those proteins. The list is chosen before seeing any data (APOE and apolipoproteins, complement C1Q/C3/C4/CFH, CLU, SERPINA3, A2M, TTR, NEFL/GFAP/YWHAG/SMOC1/SPP1/CHI3L1 and others). With n≈71 per training fold and about 1,000 proteins, this gives the model a biological prior to weight these proteins more, without dropping any of the data-driven signature. I haven't run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Drop immunoglobulin variable-region protein groups (IGHV/IGKV/IGLV) before modelling, while keeping the constant regions (IGHM, IGHA1, IGKC) that track total immunoglobulin levels. Each person's variable-region peptides come from their own antibody repertoire, so these groups vary a lot between people for reasons unrelated to AD. On deep plasma DIA there are many of them, and with n≈71 per fold they are likely adding noise to the L2 logistic regression. I chose this exclusion in advance and did not tune it against the Dev score; I haven't run it yet.

I'm averaging the current model with a second, small L2 logistic regression (C=0.1) that only sees the known-AD plasma proteins passing the filter (about 30–50 of them). Their predicted probabilities get equal weight. With about 71 training samples per fold, the full ~1,000-protein model can still pick up fold-specific noise, and a model built only from biologically chosen proteins should give a more stable ranking to anchor it. This adds a modelling component; it doesn't just reweight features, which round 11 already did, and C=0.1 and the 50/50 split were fixed in advance, not tuned.

I'm adding a third, very low-variance part to the knowledge anchor. Known AD proteins are grouped into fixed biological modules (classical complement, alternative/terminal complement, acute-phase, HDL apolipoproteins, ApoB/E lipoproteins and neuro-glial). Each sample gets one score per module: the mean of its standardised protein values in that module. A small L2 logistic regression is fitted on these 5–6 module scores. The module model and the current panel model are averaged, then mixed 50/50 with the full model as before. Averaging co-regulated proteins cancels much of the noise that comes from measuring one protein at a time, so with ~71 training samples per fold the ranking should be more stable than one built from individual proteins. I haven't run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it.

The brain-derived and glial AD markers on the prior list (GFAP, NEFL, YWHAG, SMOC1, SPP1, NPTX2, CHI3L1, and others) are low in abundance in plasma. They probably fail the 70% detection filter, so neither the full model nor the panel model ever sees them. This change lets prior-list proteins in at a lower bar: detected in at least 30% of training samples overall and within every batch. Their detection depends on abundance, so the half-minimum fill keeps the "missing because it is low" signal. Requiring detection in every batch stops those imputed blocks from encoding batch. Round 2 added missingness flags for every protein; this change only affects the prior-list proteins.

I haven't run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it. The per-batch median correction treats any difference between batches as batch effect. If the two batches hold different shares of AD cases, part of the disease signal gets subtracted along with the batch shift. This change estimates each protein's batch shift within each diagnosis class on the training fold, then averages across classes, which is ComBat's approach of including diagnosis as a covariate. Only the acquisition shift is removed and the disease difference is kept. Each batch shift is still one constant per protein, so test samples are corrected the same way and no label information reaches individual test samples. Where a batch has fewer than 3 samples of either class, it falls back to the current plain median shift.

Every gain since round 11 has come from putting prior AD biology into the model, so this round widens the a-priori biomarker list. I'm adding plasma proteins with replicated AD or amyloid links that the current list misses: fibrinogen chains, cystatin C, β2-microglobulin, IGFBP2, gelsolin, vitronectin, butyrylcholinesterase, α1-antitrypsin, angiotensinogen, paraoxonase-1 and LRG1. These are abundant, so they should pass the detection filter that blocked the low-abundance neuro-glial markers in round 15, and they reach both the weaker-penalty weighting and the compact panel model. The list comes from published literature and was not tuned against the Dev score; I haven't run this version, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Round 12 helped by dropping protein groups that vary between people for reasons unrelated to AD. This round applies the same idea to red-cell proteins: haemoglobins, carbonic anhydrases, peroxiredoxins, catalase, BLVRB, membrane-skeleton proteins and others. These enter plasma mainly through haemolysis during blood draw and handling. Because they are abundant, they pass the detection filter and add noise from sample handling to the L2 model at n≈71. Round 3 regressed contamination scores out of every protein; this change only drops the erythrocyte-specific groups themselves, using a list fixed in advance and no labels. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.

All of the recent gains came from the a-priori AD biomarker panel, but that panel is currently modelled only linearly. This adds a third ensemble member: a random forest on the same panel proteins. A forest can capture threshold effects and interactions between markers, such as an acute-phase or complement response that only matters when lipid-transport proteins are also shifted, and it ignores outliers, so its errors should differ from the two L2 logistic models. It gets a fixed 20% weight, with the two linear models at 40% each, so the stable linear signature still dominates. I chose the weights and the forest settings in advance and did not tune them against the Dev score. I haven't run this version, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

Replace the standardise + ±3 SD clip step with a rank-based inverse-normal transform fitted on the training fold. Test samples are mapped through each protein's training ECDF, with mid-rank handling for ties. This removes two things the linear models can currently lean on. First, the heavy-tailed or skewed intensity distributions that clipping only damps. Second, the arbitrary "min − 1" half-minimum fill value: tied imputed values now land at the mean normal score of the bottom quantile, which fits the "below detection" meaning without creating synthetic extremes. Everything else stays fixed: filtering, batch correction, prior weighting, the panel model and the 50/50 mix. I haven't run this version, so there is no Dev score for it yet.
